column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Every protist, from a tiny amoeba to a giant kelp, has what kind of cells?
column28: All protists are eukaryotes, so their cells have a nucleus. Many protists are tiny, so students sometimes guess prokaryotic, but prokaryotes are the bacteria.
column29: Protists are not bacteria. What do protist cells have that bacteria cells lack?

column9: Most protists are made of only one cell, which means they are ___.
column28: Unicellular means one cell. Most protists are unicellular, but not all: kelp is multicellular. Writing multicellular is the common mistake.
column29: The prefix uni- means one, as in unicycle.

column9: A student wants to collect protists to look at under a microscope. Where is the best place to collect a sample?
column14: A dry leaf from a closet
column15: Water and mud from the bottom of a pond
column17: Sand from a dry parking lot
column28: Most protists live in water or damp places, so pond water and mud is the best sample. The other places are dry, and most protists dry out and die without moisture.
column29: Think about the kind of place most protists need to live.

column9: Kingdom Protista holds the eukaryotes that do not fit into which three kingdoms?
column28: Protists are the eukaryotes that are not plants, animals or fungi. The bacteria kingdoms are prokaryotes, so they were never in the running; picking a choice with a bacteria kingdom is the common mistake.
column29: Only list kingdoms whose cells have a nucleus.

column9: What is another name for plant-like protists?
column28: Plant-like protists are called algae. Protozoans and sporozoans are animal-like protists, and slime molds are fungus-like.
column29: Think of the green scum on a pond or seaweed on a beach.

column9: The animal-like protists, such as amoebas and paramecia, are also called ___.
column28: Animal-like protists are called protozoans. Writing algae is the common mistake; algae are the plant-like protists.
column29: The word starts with proto-, meaning first.

column9: Plant-like protists use sunlight to make their own food by ___.
column28: Plant-like protists (algae) have chloroplasts and make food by photosynthesis. Respiration is the common wrong answer; it releases energy from food rather than making food.
column29: Photo- means light. Plants do the same process.

column9: Which organelle lets a green alga capture sunlight to make food?
column28: Chloroplasts capture sunlight for photosynthesis. Cilia and pseudopods are for moving, and a contractile vacuole pumps out extra water.
column29: It is the same green organelle found in plant leaves.

column9: Which word describes an organism, such as a green alga, that makes its own food?
column28: An autotroph makes its own food. Heterotroph is the common mix-up: heterotrophs take in food from other sources.
column29: Auto- means self, as in autograph.

column9: How do animal-like protists get the energy they need?
column14: They make their own food by photosynthesis, using sunlight and water
column15: They absorb sunlight through their cilia and turn it into energy
column16: They take in food, such as bacteria or bits of other organisms
column17: They make food from minerals in rocks
column28: Animal-like protists are heterotrophs: they take in food, like animals do. Only plant-like protists make food by photosynthesis, and cilia are for moving, not catching sunlight.
column29: Why are they called animal-like? Think about how animals get energy.

column9: Which protist moves using pseudopods?
column28: An amoeba moves with pseudopods (false feet). A paramecium uses cilia, *Plasmodium* can't move on its own, and kelp doesn't move around.
column29: Pseudopods are stretchy bulges, so pick the protist with no fixed shape.

column9: Short, hair-like structures that beat together in waves to push a cell through water are called ___.
column28: Cilia are short hairs that beat in waves. Flagella is the common mix-up: a flagellum is a long, whip-like tail, and there are usually only one or a few.
column29: The group of protists that uses them is named after them: the ciliates.

column9: Which description fits a flagellum?
column15: A bulge of cytoplasm that pushes forward
column16: Many short hairs covering the whole cell
column28: A flagellum is a long, whip-like tail. Many short hairs are cilia, and a bulge of cytoplasm is a pseudopod. Mixing up cilia and flagella is the common mistake.
column29: Think of how a sperm cell swims.

column9: Which of these diseases is caused by a protist?
column28: Malaria is caused by the protist *Plasmodium*. Strep throat is caused by bacteria, the flu by a virus, and athlete's foot by a fungus.
column29: This disease is a major problem in tropical countries.

column9: Diatoms are tiny golden algae. What are their shells made of?
column28: Diatom shells are made of silica, the same material as glass. Chitin is what fungus cell walls and insect skeletons are made of, so it is the tempting wrong answer.
column29: Their shells look like tiny pieces of glass under a microscope.

column9: Slime molds and water molds belong to which group of protists?
column28: Slime molds and water molds are fungus-like protists. The word mold makes many students say they are fungi, but they are protists that only look and feed like fungi.
column29: The word mold is a clue to what they resemble.

column9: How do most fungus-like protists get their food?
column14: By feeding on dead or decaying material
column16: By swimming after prey with flagella
column17: By living inside red blood cells
column28: Fungus-like protists feed on dead or decaying material, just like fungi do, which helps recycle nutrients. (A few, like the water mold that caused the potato famine, attack living hosts.) They have no chloroplasts, so photosynthesis is wrong.
column29: Think about what a mold grows on in your fridge.

column9: Giant kelp forms underwater forests off the coast of California. Which group of algae is kelp in?
column28: Kelp is a brown alga. Algae are grouped by color, and green is the tempting guess because kelp makes food, but kelp is brown.
column29: Picture the color of seaweed washed up on a beach.

column9: Every protist is made of just one cell.
column28: False. Most protists are one cell, but some, like kelp, are multicellular. Saying all protists are one cell is a common mistake.
column29: Think of a giant seaweed.

column9: Tiny algae that float near the surface of oceans and lakes are called ___.
column28: Phytoplankton are floating algae; phyto- means plant. Zooplankton are tiny floating animals and animal-like protists, so swapping the two is the common mistake.
column29: Phyto- means plant and zoo- means animal.

column9: Most protozoans reproduce asexually by one cell splitting into two. What is this called?
column28: Binary fission means splitting in two. Conjugation is when two paramecia swap genetic material, and phagocytosis is engulfing food.
column29: Binary means two.

column9: Which statement about how protists get food is correct?
column14: Some protists make their own food and others take in food
column15: All protists eat other organisms, like bacteria or bits of algae
column16: All protists make their own food, the same way that plants do
column28: Plant-like protists make their own food (autotrophs), while animal-like and fungus-like protists take in food (heterotrophs). Saying all protists are one or the other is the common mistake.
column29: Think about algae compared with amoebas.

column9: Match each protist group to how it gets food.
column14: Plant-like :: Makes its own food by photosynthesis
column15: Animal-like :: Takes in and eats other organisms
column16: Fungus-like :: Feeds on dead or decaying material
column28: Plant-like protists photosynthesize, animal-like protists eat other organisms and fungus-like protists feed on dead material. Swapping animal-like and fungus-like is the common mistake.
column29: Each group gets its food the way the organism in its name does.

column9: Match each structure to its job.
column14: Pseudopod :: A "false foot" that stretches out to move and trap food
column15: Cilia :: Short hairs that beat in waves
column16: Flagellum :: A long, whip-like tail that pushes or pulls the cell
column17: Chloroplast :: Captures sunlight to make food
column28: Pseudopods are false feet, cilia are short hairs, a flagellum is a long tail and a chloroplast makes food. Mixing up cilia and flagella is the most common mistake.
column29: Start with chloroplast, then sort the three ways to move by length.

column9: Amoebas, kelp and slime molds all belong to which kingdom?
column28: All three are protists. Kelp looks like a plant and slime molds look like fungi, which is why students pick Plantae or Fungi, but all three are eukaryotes that don't fit those kingdoms.
column29: Which kingdom holds very different eukaryotes that don't fit anywhere else?

column9: Select every organism that is a protist. Select all that apply.
column28: Paramecium, diatoms and *Plasmodium* are protists. Yeast is a one-celled fungus, so choosing it because it is one cell is the common mistake. Oak trees are plants, and staph is a bacterium.
column29: Cross out the plant, the bacterium and the fungus used to make bread.

column9: Which word describes an organism like *Plasmodium* that lives in or on another organism and harms it?
column28: A parasite lives in or on a host and harms it, like *Plasmodium* in a person. A decomposer breaks down dead things, which is the common mix-up.
column29: The host is alive and is being hurt.

column9: Which description fits the sporozoans, the group that includes *Plasmodium*?
column15: They crawl through the blood with pseudopods, like amoebas do
column16: They make their own food with chloroplasts, even while living inside a host
column17: They are parasites that can't move on their own and reproduce by spores
column28: Sporozoans are parasites with no way to move and reproduce by spores. The name sporozoan comes from spore. Picking pseudopods mixes them up with sarcodines.
column29: Look at the first part of the word sporozoan.

column9: The paramecium belongs to which group of animal-like protists?
column28: A paramecium is covered with cilia, so it is a ciliate. Sarcodines like the amoeba use pseudopods, and flagellates use flagella.
column29: Animal-like protists are named for how they move. How does a paramecium move?

column9: Which kind of algae is common in ponds and is the closest relative of land plants?
column28: Green algae are the algae most closely related to land plants, and they are common in fresh water. Brown algae (kelp) are big, so students sometimes pick them, but they live in the ocean.
column29: Land plants and these algae use the same kinds of chlorophyll and both store food as starch.

column9: What is the main difference between a protist and a bacterium?
column15: A bacterium has a nucleus and a protist does not
column16: A protist has a nucleus and a bacterium does not
column28: Protists are eukaryotes with a nucleus; bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus. Both have DNA. Reversing the two is the common mistake.
column29: Think eukaryote versus prokaryote.

column9: The word "protozoa" means "first ___."
column28: Protozoa means first animals, because these protists eat and move the way animals do. They are not actually animals; they are protists.
column29: Zoo- is the same root as in zoology and zoo.

column9: Red algae are used to make nori, the dark sheets wrapped around sushi. How do red algae get their energy?
column14: By living inside other organisms' blood
column28: Red algae are plant-like protists, so they make food by photosynthesis. Their color is red because of extra pigments, not because they eat other things; that is the common mistake.
column29: All algae, whatever their color, are the same type of protist.

column9: Why are phytoplankton so important to ocean animals?
column14: They are the food at the base of ocean food chains
column15: They cause disease in whales and other large sea animals
column16: They hunt small fish, which keeps fish numbers in check
column28: Phytoplankton are producers: they make food that zooplankton eat, which feed fish and larger animals. Students sometimes think tiny organisms can't matter, but the whole ocean food chain rests on them.
column29: Phytoplankton make their own food. Who eats them?

column9: Which insect spreads African sleeping sickness to people?
column28: The tsetse fly spreads the flagellate *Trypanosoma*, which causes African sleeping sickness. The *Anopheles* mosquito spreads malaria, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Malaria and sleeping sickness are spread by different biting insects.

column9: What happens inside an amoeba's food vacuole?
column28: A food vacuole is a sac where food is digested. DNA is stored in the nucleus, and amoebas have no chloroplasts to capture sunlight.
column29: The name of the vacuole tells you what goes into it.

column9: Which of these is an animal-like protist?
column28: An amoeba takes in food and moves, so it is animal-like. Kelp and diatoms are plant-like algae, and the slime mold is fungus-like.
column29: Which one hunts and eats its food?

column9: A protozoan that swims with one or more long, whip-like tails is called a(n) ___.
column28: Protozoans with flagella are flagellates. Ciliate is the common mix-up; ciliates have many short hairs, not long tails.
column29: Take the name of the long tail and turn it into a group name.

column9: In the 1840s, a protist destroyed Ireland's potato crops and caused a famine. What kind of protist was it?
column28: A water mold, a fungus-like protist, caused the potato blight. Students often say it was a fungus, but water molds are protists.
column29: It was a fungus-like protist that grows in damp conditions.

column9: Put the steps of an amoeba catching its food in order.
column14: The bulges meet and close around the food
column15: The amoeba moves toward a bit of food
column16: The food ends up trapped in a vacuole inside the cell
column17: Bulges of cytoplasm stretch out on both sides of the food
column28: The amoeba moves to the food, stretches out pseudopods around it, closes them and traps the food in a food vacuole. A common slip is putting the vacuole step before the bulges close.
column29: The amoeba has to reach the food before it can wrap around it.

column9: When a protist wraps parts of its cell around a bit of food and pulls it inside, the process is called ___.
column28: Phagocytosis means cell eating: the cell surrounds food and takes it in. Conjugation is swapping genetic material, and binary fission is splitting in two.
column29: Phago- means eat, and -cyto- means cell.

column9: Select every structure that a protozoan might use to move. Select all that apply.
column28: Protozoans move with pseudopods, cilia or flagella. Chloroplasts make food, food vacuoles digest food and protists have no roots. Missing pseudopods because they aren't a permanent part is a common slip.
column29: There are three ways protozoans move: false feet, short hairs and long tails.

column9: Which feature tells you a protist is plant-like rather than animal-like?
column28: Chloroplasts mean it makes its own food, so it is plant-like. Every protist has a nucleus, and both types can be one cell and live in water, so those don't tell them apart.
column29: Pick the feature that only one of the two groups has.

column9: Match each protist to its type.
column28: Kelp is an alga (plant-like), a paramecium eats and swims (animal-like) and a slime mold feeds on decaying material (fungus-like). Calling kelp a true plant is the common mistake.
column29: Ask: does it make food, eat food or feed on dead material?

column9: *Plasmodium* swims through the blood using cilia.
column28: False. *Plasmodium* is a sporozoan, and sporozoans can't move on their own. It is carried by blood. Ciliates, like the paramecium, are the ones with cilia.
column29: Which group of protozoans has no way to move itself?

column9: A single green cell scraped from a damp tree trunk has a nucleus and chloroplasts. Which kingdom does it most likely belong to?
column14: Eubacteria, because it is one cell
column15: Fungi, because it lives in a damp place
column16: Plantae, because it has chloroplasts and makes its own food from sunlight
column17: Protista, because it is a one-celled eukaryote with chloroplasts
column28: A single cell with a nucleus is a eukaryote, and a one-celled eukaryote with chloroplasts is a green alga, a protist. Plants are multicellular, so choosing Plantae just because of chloroplasts is the common mistake.
column29: It has a nucleus, so rule out bacteria. Then ask: can a plant be just one cell?

column9: A biologist finds a one-celled organism in a lake. Its cell has no nucleus. Could it be a protist?
column14: No, because protists are eukaryotes; it is probably a bacterium
column15: Yes, because it lives in water, where most protists are found
column17: No, because protists are always multicellular and this organism is one cell
column28: Every protist has a nucleus, so a cell with no nucleus is a prokaryote, most likely a bacterium. Being small and living in water fit many organisms and are the tempting wrong reasons.
column29: What do all protists have in their cells?

column9: Under the microscope, a cell keeps changing shape. It pushes out bulges toward a bit of food and its cytoplasm flows into them. Which organism is it?
column28: Changing shape and pushing out bulges (pseudopods) is how an amoeba moves. A paramecium keeps a slipper shape and uses cilia, and *Trypanosoma* uses a flagellum.
column29: Which protist has no fixed shape?

column9: A slipper-shaped cell in pond water is covered with tiny hairs that beat back and forth, and it spins as it swims. Which organism is it?
column28: A slipper shape with hairs (cilia) all over is a paramecium. An amoeba has no fixed shape, kelp doesn't swim and *Plasmodium* can't move on its own.
column29: Which protist is famous for being shaped like a slipper?

column9: Select every protist that is an autotroph. Select all that apply.
column28: Diatoms and *Spirogyra* are algae with chloroplasts, so they make their own food. Amoebas and paramecia eat food, *Plasmodium* takes food from its host and slime molds feed on decaying material. Thinking every protist in water photosynthesizes is the common mistake.
column29: Autotrophs make their own food. Which ones are algae?

column9: Select every disease that is caused by a protist. Select all that apply.
column28: Malaria (*Plasmodium*), sleeping sickness (*Trypanosoma*) and amoebic dysentery (*Entamoeba*) are protist diseases. Strep throat and tuberculosis are caused by bacteria, and the flu by a virus.
column29: One of the protist diseases has the name of a protist in it.

column9: Match each protozoan to its group.
column28: The amoeba moves with pseudopods (sarcodine), the paramecium with cilia (ciliate), *Trypanosoma* with a flagellum (flagellate) and *Plasmodium* can't move and makes spores (sporozoan). Mixing up ciliates and flagellates is the common mistake.
column29: Think about how each one moves, or if it can move at all.

column9: Health workers in parts of Africa give families bed nets treated with insecticide. How do the nets help fight malaria?
column14: They kill the *Plasmodium* already in a sleeping person's blood, curing the disease
column15: They filter protists out of drinking water
column16: They keep tsetse flies, which carry *Plasmodium*, from biting people at night
column17: They block bites from *Anopheles* mosquitoes, which carry *Plasmodium*
column28: Malaria spreads when an *Anopheles* mosquito carries *Plasmodium* from one person to another, so stopping bites at night breaks the chain. Nets don't cure someone who is already sick, and tsetse flies spread a different disease.
column29: How does *Plasmodium* get from one person to the next?

column9: Which pair of protists are BOTH heterotrophs?
column28: Paramecia and amoebas are animal-like protists that take in food, so both are heterotrophs. Diatoms, kelp and green algae all have chloroplasts and make their own food, so any pair with an alga is wrong.
column29: Heterotrophs must take in food. Cross out every alga.

column9: Put these events in the spread of malaria in order.
column14: *Plasmodium* enters red blood cells and multiplies
column15: A mosquito bites a person who has malaria and takes in *Plasmodium* with the blood
column16: The red blood cells burst, releasing more *Plasmodium*
column17: The same mosquito bites a healthy person, and *Plasmodium* enters that person's blood
column28: The mosquito picks up *Plasmodium* from a sick person, passes it to a healthy person, *Plasmodium* invades red blood cells and multiplies, and then the cells burst. Starting with the healthy person is the common slip; the mosquito must pick it up first.
column29: The mosquito can't pass on *Plasmodium* until it has picked it up.

column9: Two paramecia line up side by side, swap some genetic material and then separate. What is this process called?
column28: Conjugation is when two paramecia exchange genetic material. Binary fission is the tempting wrong answer, but in binary fission one cell splits into two and nothing is swapped.
column29: No new cells are made here; two cells join for a while and then part.

column9: A single paramecium splits into two, then each new cell splits into two, and so on. After 3 rounds of splitting, how many paramecia are there?
column28: Each round doubles the number: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. A common mistake is adding 2 each round (getting 6) instead of doubling.
column29: Write out the number after each round. Each round, every cell splits.

column9: In late summer, fertilizer washes from farm fields into a lake, and the water turns bright green. Which protists most likely caused the green color?
column15: Slime molds growing on the lake bottom
column16: Green algae multiplying with the extra nutrients
column28: Fertilizer adds nutrients, and green algae use them to grow quickly, turning the water green (an algal bloom). Amoebas are not green and don't make food, so they can't color the water.
column29: Which protists are green and grow when given extra nutrients?

column9: On a hike, you find a bright yellow, slimy blob slowly creeping across a rotting log. What is it most likely?
column28: A slimy blob that creeps over rotting wood is a slime mold, a fungus-like protist. Mushrooms don't move, so calling it a mushroom is the common mistake.
column29: Fungi stay in one place. What on this list can creep?

column9: Amoebic dysentery is a disease of the intestines. How do people usually catch it?
column14: Drinking water or eating food contaminated with the amoeba
column16: Being bitten by a tsetse fly
column17: Breathing in spores from slime molds that grow on damp, rotting logs
column28: The amoeba that causes dysentery spreads through dirty water or food. Mosquito bites spread malaria and tsetse fly bites spread sleeping sickness, which are the common mix-ups.
column29: It is a disease of the intestines. How do things get into your intestines?

column9: Put these ocean organisms in order in a food chain, starting with the producer.
column28: Diatoms make their own food, zooplankton eat diatoms, herring eat zooplankton and seals eat herring. Starting with zooplankton is the common mistake; they are consumers, not producers.
column29: Find the organism that makes its own food. That is the start.

column9: Which group of organisms makes a large share of the oxygen in Earth's air, even though you can't see them without a microscope?
column28: Phytoplankton are algae that photosynthesize and release oxygen, and there are so many of them that they make a large share of Earth's oxygen. Many students think land plants make it all.
column29: Oxygen is released by photosynthesis. Which of these photosynthesize?

column9: A student says, "Kelp is a plant because it is big, makes its own food and grows in the ocean." Which is the best correction?
column14: Kelp is a fungus, because it lives in a damp place and has no flowers or seeds
column15: Kelp is an animal, because it sways and moves with the ocean waves
column16: Kelp is an alga, which is a protist; it has no true roots, stems or leaves
column17: Kelp is a bacterium because it is simple
column28: Kelp is a large alga, a plant-like protist. It makes food like a plant but lacks true roots, stems and leaves. Thinking that making food automatically makes something a plant is the common mistake.
column29: Plant-like does not mean plant. What is missing from kelp?

column9: *Euglena* has a red eyespot. How does the eyespot help it?
column14: It stores extra DNA so the cell can copy itself faster
column15: It digests the food that *Euglena* takes in from the water
column17: It senses light so *Euglena* can swim toward it
column28: The eyespot senses light, and *Euglena* swims toward light so its chloroplasts can make food. It is not a real eye that sees images, and it does not digest food.
column29: *Euglena* has chloroplasts. What does it need to find?

column9: A paramecium living in a freshwater pond keeps taking in extra water. Which structure collects the extra water and pumps it out?
column28: The contractile vacuole collects extra water and squeezes it out so the cell doesn't burst. The food vacuole is the common mix-up; it digests food.
column29: Contract means squeeze.

column9: Hikers who drink untreated stream water can get sick from *Giardia*, a flagellate that causes diarrhea. What is the best way to prevent it?
column14: Wear insect repellent to keep biting flies away
column15: Boil or filter the water before drinking it
column17: Avoid touching plants and rocks along the stream banks
column28: *Giardia* spreads through water, so boiling or filtering water kills or removes it. Insect repellent prevents diseases spread by bites, like malaria, not waterborne ones.
column29: How does *Giardia* get into a hiker's body?

column9: Select every statement that is true of a paramecium. Select all that apply.
column28: A paramecium is a one-celled eukaryote that eats food, so it is a heterotroph with a nucleus. It has no chloroplasts, moves with cilia (not pseudopods) and is not a prokaryote.
column29: It is an animal-like protist. What do all protists have, and how do animal-like ones get food?

column9: When a paramecium splits into two cells asexually, how do the two new cells compare with the original cell?
column14: They are a mix of DNA from two parents
column15: They each have half of the original's DNA
column16: They are genetically identical to the original
column28: Splitting in two is asexual, so the DNA is copied first and each new cell gets a full, identical set. Mixing DNA from two parents only happens in sexual processes, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Asexual reproduction has only one parent.

column9: Kelp forests give shelter and food to fish, sea otters and many other animals. Which role does kelp play in this ecosystem?
column28: Kelp makes its own food by photosynthesis, so it is a producer. Decomposers break down dead material, which is the common mix-up for anything that is not an animal.
column29: Kelp is an alga. How does it get its food?

column9: A scientist cuts an amoeba in two. The half with the nucleus keeps living and later divides. The half without the nucleus stops eating and eventually dies. What does this show?
column14: The nucleus controls the cell's activities
column15: The nucleus is where the amoeba's food is made and stored
column17: Cutting a cell in half makes both halves reproduce faster
column28: Only the half with the nucleus could keep living and divide, so the nucleus controls the cell. Food is made in chloroplasts, not the nucleus, and amoebas have no chloroplasts.
column29: What did the surviving half have that the other half didn't?

column9: Organisms that cannot make their own food and must take it in from their surroundings are called ___.
column28: Heterotrophs (also called consumers) take in food. Autotroph is the common mix-up; autotrophs make their own food.
column29: Hetero- means other: they get food from other sources.

column9: Amoebas and paramecia are called "animal-like" even though they are not animals. Why?
column15: Like animals, they take in food and most can move, but each is only one cell
column16: They make their own food like animals do, and they can move around on their own
column28: They eat and move like animals, but they are single cells with no tissues or organs, so they are protists. Animals don't make their own food, so that choice is wrong.
column29: What do animals do to get food, and how many cells are these protists?

column9: Red tides happen when huge numbers of dinoflagellates bloom in coastal water. Most dinoflagellates have chloroplasts. What kind of protist are they?
column28: Having chloroplasts means they make their own food, so dinoflagellates are plant-like protists (algae). Their red color fools students, but color doesn't change how they get food.
column29: Use the chloroplast clue.

column9: A student finds white, cottony fuzz growing on a dead fish in an aquarium. It absorbs nutrients from the dead fish. Which protist is it most likely?
column28: Fuzzy growth that feeds on dead material in water is a water mold, a fungus-like protist. Green algae make their own food, and sporozoans live inside living hosts.
column29: It lives in water and looks like mold.

column9: Which observation best tells a sarcodine apart from a ciliate under a microscope?
column14: Whether it moves with pseudopods or with many short hairs
column15: Whether it lives in fresh water or in salty ocean water
column16: Whether it has a nucleus holding its DNA, or has no nucleus
column28: Protozoan groups are sorted by how they move, so the way it moves tells them apart. Both have a nucleus, both live in water and both are one cell, so those don't help.
column29: Pick the trait the two groups do NOT share.

column9: Slime molds look like fungi, but biologists put them in Kingdom Protista. Select every observation that supports this. Select all that apply.
column14: Slime molds can creep along the ground during part of their life
column15: Slime molds engulf bacteria and bits of food, much like an amoeba does
column16: Slime molds make their food with chloroplasts
column18: Slime molds have cell walls made of chitin, just like mushrooms
column28: Fungi can't move and don't engulf food, so creeping and engulfing food are not fungus traits. Slime molds have no chloroplasts, they do have a nucleus, and chitin walls would make them more like fungi, not less.
column29: Look for things a mushroom can never do.

column9: A pond sample starts with 5 amoebas. Each amoeba splits into two every 12 hours, and none die. How many amoebas will there be after 2 days?
column28: 2 days is 48 hours, which is 4 splits of 12 hours. 5 → 10 → 20 → 40 → 80. A common mistake is counting only 2 splits (one per day), which gives 20.
column29: First find how many 12-hour periods are in 2 days.

column9: A student counts paramecia in a culture: 10 on Monday, 20 on Tuesday and 40 on Wednesday. If the number keeps doubling each day, how many will there be on Friday?
column28: Doubling each day: Thursday 80, Friday 160. A common mistake is adding 20 each day or stopping at Thursday's 80.
column29: Keep doubling one day at a time until you reach Friday.

column9: A biologist seals two pond protists in separate clear dishes with only water, air and light (no other food). After two weeks, protist X is thriving and protist Y has died. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: X is probably a sporozoan living off the water, and Y is probably an alga that ran out of light
column15: X probably makes its own food like a plant-like protist; Y probably needed to take in food
column17: Y probably had more chloroplasts than X, so it used up the light faster and died
column28: With only light and no food, only an autotroph could make its own food and survive. Y died, so it likely needed to take in food. Choosing that Y was an alga reverses the evidence.
column29: Which kind of protist can live on light alone?

column9: A student claims, "All protists are tiny, one-celled organisms." Which fact best disproves the claim?
column16: Giant kelp is a multicellular protist that can grow over 30 meters long
column17: *Plasmodium* is a protist that lives inside human red blood cells and liver cells
column28: One large, multicellular protist is enough to prove the claim wrong. The other facts are true but are about one-celled protists, so they don't disprove it.
column29: To disprove "all," you need just one example that doesn't fit.

column9: A traveler comes home from a tropical country with fevers and chills that return every two to three days. A blood test shows parasites inside the red blood cells. Which protist is most likely, and how was it most likely caught?
column15: An amoeba, from swimming in a lake
column28: Parasites in red blood cells and fevers that come and go are signs of malaria, caused by *Plasmodium* and spread by mosquitoes. The fevers repeat when red blood cells burst. *Trypanosoma* is also spread by an insect bite, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.
column29: Which protist hides and multiplies in red blood cells?

column9: Mosquitoes carry *Plasmodium* from one person to the next. Which town plan would do the most to cut down on malaria?
column14: Drain standing water where mosquitoes lay their eggs
column15: Boil all drinking water before people use it
column16: Wash all fruits and vegetables before they are sold or eaten
column17: Spray the fields around town to kill tsetse flies
column28: Fewer mosquitoes means fewer chances to carry *Plasmodium* between people. Malaria does not spread through water or food, so boiling water and washing food help with other diseases, not this one.
column29: Attack the carrier where it breeds.

column9: Fresh pond water keeps seeping into a paramecium, and the paramecium survives by pumping the extra water back out. If it is moved to water that is a little saltier (closer to the saltiness inside the cell), what should happen to its pumping?
column14: It pumps more often, because more water enters
column15: It pumps less often, because less water enters
column16: It stops eating and grows chloroplasts
column17: Nothing changes, because the pumping has nothing to do with water
column28: Water seeps in because the pond water is much less salty than the cell. If the outside water is closer to the cell's saltiness, less water moves in, so the cell needs to pump less. Thinking salt makes it pump more is the common mistake.
column29: Water moves in because the cell is saltier than fresh water. What if that difference shrinks?

column9: A student is not sure whether an unknown cell is a bacterium or a protist. Select every observation that shows it is NOT a bacterium. Select all that apply.
column18: It has a food vacuole and other membrane-bound organelles
column28: Only eukaryotes have a nucleus, chloroplasts and other membrane-bound organelles. Bacteria are also single cells, live in water and are small, so those observations don't rule them out. Some bacteria photosynthesize, but they don't have chloroplasts.
column29: Look for things that only eukaryotic cells have.

column9: Match each protist to the disease it causes.
column17: *Phytophthora infestans* :: Late blight, which wiped out Ireland's potatoes
column28: *Plasmodium* causes malaria, *Trypanosoma* causes sleeping sickness, *Entamoeba* (an amoeba, as its name hints) causes amoebic dysentery and the water mold *Phytophthora* destroyed Ireland's potatoes. Swapping *Plasmodium* and *Trypanosoma* is the common mistake.
column29: Look inside each name for clues: *Entamoeba* has "amoeba" in it.

column9: A protozoan reproduces asexually by splitting in two. Put the steps in order.
column14: The cell pinches in at the middle
column28: The DNA is copied first, then the nucleus divides, the cell pinches in and the two new cells separate. Putting the pinching before the nucleus divides is the common mistake; each new cell needs its own nucleus first.
column29: Each new cell will need its own copy of DNA. When must that happen?

column9: Water molds look like fuzzy fungi. Why do biologists place them in Kingdom Protista instead?
column14: Water molds make their own food with chloroplasts, the way plant-like algae do in ponds
column15: Water molds have no nucleus, so they are too simple to be true fungi
column16: Water molds have cellulose cell walls, not chitin, and some spores swim with flagella
column17: Water molds are animals because they live in water
column28: True fungi have chitin cell walls and no swimming cells. Water molds have cellulose walls and swimming spores, so they are fungus-like protists. They have no chloroplasts and do have a nucleus.
column29: What are fungus cell walls made of?

column9: Use this key to classify a protist. 1a: Has chloroplasts → plant-like. 1b: No chloroplasts → go to 2. 2a: Moves and takes in food → animal-like. 2b: Does not move for most of its life and grows as threads or a slimy mass → fungus-like. A protist with no chloroplasts grows as a mat of fuzzy threads on a dead insect floating in a pond. Where does the key place it?
column28: No chloroplasts sends you to step 2. It grows as threads and doesn't move around hunting food, so 2b: fungus-like (a water mold). Stopping at step 1 and guessing is the common mistake.
column29: Follow the key one step at a time.

column9: A student designs an experiment to test whether *Euglena* needs light to grow. Which design is best?
column14: Use two identical *Euglena* dishes, one in light and one in the dark, and count cells after a week
column15: Put one dish in the light and count the cells after one hour
column16: Put one dish in the light at 25 °C and another in the dark at 10 °C, then count the cells after a week
column17: Add food to the dark dish only and see which grows more
column28: A fair test changes only one variable (light) and keeps everything else the same, with enough time to see growth. Changing the temperature or the food too means you can't tell what caused the difference.
column29: Only one thing should be different between the dishes.

column9: *Euglena* has chloroplasts, but in the dark it can take in food from the water. It also swims with a flagellum. Why is *Euglena* hard to place into just one protist group?
column14: It has no nucleus, so it might be a bacterium like the cyanobacteria
column15: It has traits of both plant-like protists and animal-like protists
column16: It is multicellular, like a plant
column17: It absorbs dead material from the water, like a fungus-like protist does
column28: *Euglena* can make food like algae and take in food and swim like protozoans, so it fits two groups. It is one cell with a nucleus, so it is not a bacterium or a multicellular plant, and it does not live by feeding on dead material like a fungus-like protist.
column29: List what *Euglena* does that algae do, then what protozoans do.

column9: Two test tubes hold the same pond water full of green algae. Tube A sits in bright light and fills with tiny gas bubbles. Tube B sits in the dark and makes almost no bubbles. What is the best explanation?
column14: The algae in tube B are making more oxygen but holding it in
column15: The algae in tube A are digesting food in food vacuoles
column16: The algae in tube A are photosynthesizing and releasing oxygen
column17: The light is making the water boil
column28: In light, algae photosynthesize and give off oxygen gas, which forms the bubbles. In the dark there is no photosynthesis. Bright light alone does not boil water, which is a common guess.
column29: What gas do algae give off, and what do they need to make it?

column9: A classmate says, "Protists are harmful, so it would be better if they all disappeared." Which response is best?
column14: That's right; every protist causes disease in people, animals or crops
column15: Only algae are harmful, because their blooms turn lakes green, so only they should disappear
column16: Protists can't affect people at all
column17: Only a few cause disease; algae feed ocean food chains and make much of Earth's oxygen
column28: A few protists cause disease, but algae are producers that feed ocean life and release oxygen. Thinking of protists only as germs is the common mistake.
column29: Think about what algae do for the rest of life on Earth.

column9: A scientist discovers a new ocean organism. It is made of many eukaryotic cells and has chloroplasts, but it has no roots, stems, leaves or specialized tissues. Which kingdom does it most likely belong to?
column28: Without roots, stems, leaves or specialized tissues, it is not a plant. A multicellular eukaryote with chloroplasts but simple body is an alga, a protist. Choosing Plantae because of the chloroplasts is the common mistake.
column29: Plants have true roots, stems and leaves. Does this organism?

column9: In a northern Wisconsin lake, the number of algae rises in spring and summer and drops in winter. What is the best explanation?
column14: Algae eat more bacteria in summer, when warm water helps bacteria multiply
column15: More hours of sunlight in spring and summer allow more photosynthesis
column16: Algae hibernate in winter like bears, then wake up when the ice melts
column17: Cold water gives algae more food
column28: Algae make food by photosynthesis, so more sunlight means more food and more growth. In winter, short days and ice cover cut the light. Thinking algae eat other organisms is the common mistake.
column29: What do algae need from the environment to make food?

column9: Select every pair in which the protist is correctly matched with how it gets food. Select all that apply.
column16: Slime mold: feeds on decaying leaves and logs
column18: Diatom: absorbs nutrients from dead animals
column28: Kelp photosynthesizes, an amoeba engulfs food and a slime mold feeds on decaying material. *Plasmodium* is a parasite with no chloroplasts, and a diatom is an alga that photosynthesizes.
column29: Sort each protist into plant-like, animal-like or fungus-like first.

column9: Why do many scientists say Kingdom Protista is not a "natural" group the way Kingdom Animalia is?
column14: Protists have no DNA, so scientists cannot compare them to see how closely related they are
column16: They are lumped together for not fitting other kingdoms, so many aren't close relatives
column28: Protista collects eukaryotes that aren't plants, animals or fungi, so its members are very different and many aren't close relatives. Protists do have DNA and a nucleus.
column29: Think about how the kingdom is defined: by what protists are NOT.

column9: A student classifies a protist as plant-like because it is green and lives in a pond. Under high power, the green turns out to be algae it has eaten, packed into its food vacuoles. It has no chloroplasts of its own. How should it be classified?
column14: Plant-like, because it is green and lives in a sunny pond like algae
column15: Not a protist at all, because protists cannot eat other protists
column16: Fungus-like, because it lives in water
column17: Animal-like, because it takes in food and has no chloroplasts
column28: It eats other organisms and has no chloroplasts, so it is a heterotroph: an animal-like protist. Its color came from its food. Using color instead of how it gets food is the mistake the student made.
column29: What matters is how it gets food, not what color it looks.

column9: A protist from a ditch is examined. Select every observation that would support classifying it as an animal-like protist. Select all that apply.
column17: It forms a food vacuole around its food
column18: It grows as a fuzzy mat on dead insects
column28: Eating bacteria, moving with cilia and forming food vacuoles are animal-like traits. Chloroplasts point to plant-like and a fuzzy mat on dead insects points to fungus-like. Every protist has a nucleus, so the nucleus doesn't support one group over another; picking it is the common mistake.
column29: Pick only traits that separate animal-like protists from the other two groups.

column9: In the ocean, phytoplankton are eaten by zooplankton, which are eaten by small fish, which are eaten by tuna. A warm-water event kills a large share of the phytoplankton. What would most likely happen to the tuna over the next months?
column14: Tuna would decline because less food moves up the food chain
column15: Tuna would increase because phytoplankton compete with them
column16: Tuna would not change because they don't eat phytoplankton
column28: Fewer producers means less food for zooplankton, then fewer small fish, then less food for tuna. Thinking tuna are safe because they don't eat phytoplankton directly is the common mistake.
column29: Trace the energy one step at a time from the phytoplankton to the tuna.

column9: Under a microscope, a student sees a cell with a nucleus and a single long, whip-like tail swimming among red blood cells. The sample came from a patient who got sick after a tsetse fly bite. Which protist is it most likely?
column28: A whip-like tail is a flagellum, and the tsetse fly carries the flagellate *Trypanosoma*. *Plasmodium* is also a blood parasite, but it can't swim and is spread by mosquitoes.
column29: Two clues: how it moves and which insect carried it.
